An upper trough is beginning to impact the Northern Rockies as it
progresses through the Mountain West into the new week. This 
system will bring an abundance of atmospheric moisture to the 
region, with precipitable water anomalies of nearly 300% over 
southeast Montana into Monday. The liquid precipitation forecast 
is shown as an extreme event for this time of year, with the ECMWF
EFI (Extreme Forecast Index) displaying values of 0.8 to 1.0 
(with 1 being the maximum). Values of 0.8 or greater signify an 
extreme or very unusual event. More on this shortly.

Showers have begun to develop over south-central Montana and will
continue to spread across the entire forecast area through this 
afternoon and last into Monday. Widespread rainfall is expected, 
while snowfall will occur in the mountains. Moderate to heavy 
rainfall is expected south and east of Billings where there 0.75 
to 1.5 inches of rainfall is forecast. The latest probability for 
greater than 1 inch of rainfall is 60 to 90% for portions of Big 
Horn and Treasure Counties and all counties to the east. The 
probability for at least 2 inches of rainfall for the same area is
10 to 30%. For portions of northern Wyoming, rainfall up to or 
greater than an inch are possible although confidence is lower. 
This is partly do to a developing surface low in southern Wyoming 
that may result in some drier periods over the next 24 hours. The 
probability for at least a half inch remains high (60 to 85%) 
though. For the rest of south-central Montana several tenths of 
an inch of rainfall are in the forecast, though amounts are lower 
going north and west of Billings. The probability for at least 
half an inch of rain is 40 to 90% (greatest around Billings and 
the Absaroka/Beartooth foothills).

Circling back to the EFI discussion, the single day precipitation
record for the Miles City Airport in November is 1.17" on 
November 1st of 1957. For the upcoming event, the forecast has 1 
to 1.4 inches of rainfall in the Miles City area. It does not 
appear as though KMLS will set a new single day record, as several
tenths of an inch of rain are forecast for this evening splitting
the storm total across the first two days of the month. While a 
single day record for KMLS looks unlikely, the average 
precipitation total for the month of November at KMLS from 1990 to
2020 was 0.33". Across the entire period of record for KMLS 
(records began in 1937), the average for November is 0.42". In 
other words, this is going to be a very wet month after just 2 
days.

For Sheridan, the single day November precipitation record 
occurred on November 9th, 1978 when 0.85" of precipitation fell. 
For this event around 3/4 of an inch are forecast for Monday. A 
single day record could be broken. For the month overall, the 
average from 1990 to 2020 was 0.76". The period of record goes 
back to 1907 and the average since then is 0.78". KSHR may surpass
the monthly average after two days as well.

In the mountains, snowfall will begin tonight and last through 
Monday afternoon. North and west aspects of the 
Absaroka/Beartooths and the Bighorns will be favored. This system 
will not bring much cold air with it, although snow levels drop as
low as 5,500 feet Monday morning. A rain/snow mix will start in 
the high country before transitioning to all snow tonight. For the
Absaroka/Beartooths, 4 to 8 inches of snowfall are forecast 
though locally higher amounts are possible. In the Pryors, up to 4
inches are forecast. For the Bighorns, 5 to 10 inches are 
forecast with locally higher amounts possible. The majority of 
accumulations in the Absaroka/Beartooth and Bighorn Mountains will
fall above 7,500 feet. With snow levels as low as 5,500 feet, 
foothill locations such as Red Lodge could see some light snowfall
as well although accumulations will be minimal (less than an 
inch).

A cold front is expected to move across the area tonight into 
Monday, this will bring widespread breezy north-northwest winds 
with gusts in the 20s to 40 mph. Windier conditions are forecast 
for southeast Montana and northern Wyoming with gusts in the 40s 
to low 50s mph. The probability for gusts of 50 mph or greater in 
Sheridan County is 40 to 90%, greatest along the Johnson County 
line. The probability for gusts greater than 60 mph in Sheridan 
County is around 20 to 40%, almost exclusively along the Johnson 
County line. For locations in southeast Montana, the probability 
for 50 mph is 40 to 80% along and east of State Highway 323 and 
greatest along the border. The probability for 60 mph winds is 20%
or less.

will result in very difficult conditions for those traveling along
Highway 14, as well as those in the back country. Because of
